patients.summary: Retired math teacher with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, stable angina and giant cell arteritis on long-term prednisone who joins in 2020. From 2023 he accumulates vascular events: recurrent BPH symptoms, ischemic colitis with an incidental AAA, a post-catheterization groin fistula, cholesterol emboli with kidney injury, an adhesive bowel obstruction, mesenteric ischemia after EVAR, and a type A aortic dissection repaired in February 2026.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
68 y/o retired HS math teacher establishing care. Previous PCP retired and the practice closed, he heard about us through a neighbor.

PMH
- HTN, many years, on amlodipine. Home readings 130s/80s.
- Hyperlipidemia on atorvastatin 40.
- CAD with stable angina. Gets a tight feeling in the chest walking up the long hill by the reservoir, goes away when he stops. Pattern unchanged for years. Followed by an outside cardiology group, managed with meds, never stented.
- Giant cell arteritis dx 2019 by outside rheumatology, on prednisone 10 mg daily since. Sees rheum about yearly. No headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or visual change since.
- BPH dx years ago, got up at night for a while, settled on its own. Not on anything.

PSH: appendectomy around age 45. Lap cholecystectomy before that, he can't remember the year.

Meds: aspirin 81, atorvastatin 40, amlodipine 5, prednisone 10 (rheum prescribes).
Allergies: none known.

FH: father MI at 68, also HTN. Mother stroke at 75, high cholesterol. Uncle on mother's side had an AAA.
SH: lives alone in Westfield. Never smoked. A beer or a glass of wine once or twice a week. Retired from teaching algebra and calculus, tutors a little. Walks most days.

ROS: no chest pain at rest, no dyspnea, no claudication, no urinary complaints currently, no GI complaints, no weight change.

Exam: vitals as charted. Well appearing. No temporal artery tenderness, pulses present. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, healed scars. No edema, pedal pulses intact.

A/P
1. HTN: at goal on amlodipine 5. Continue.
2. HLD/CAD: atorvastatin 40, aspirin. Lipids today. Angina stable, keeps seeing cardiology.
3. GCA on prednisone 10: per rheum. ESR/CRP today for our baseline.
4. BPH: quiet.
5. Health maintenance: will request old records for colonoscopy and vaccines. Flu shot next month with the nurse.

RTC 6 months.

documents.title: Lab results released
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Mr. Graves, your labs from Tuesday look good. Kidney function, liver tests, blood count and sugar are normal. LDL cholesterol is 82, which is fine on your current atorvastatin. Your inflammation markers (ESR and CRP) are normal, consistent with the GCA being quiet. No changes.

Scanned to chart, routed to PCP.

Outside rheumatology group
Date of visit: 11/19/2020

Dear colleague,

I saw Mr. Graves, 68, in follow-up of giant cell arteritis diagnosed in 2019. He has had no headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms or shoulder and hip girdle stiffness. He continues prednisone 10 mg each morning.

Exam: temporal arteries nontender with normal pulsation. No bruits over the subclavian arteries. Normal shoulder and hip range.

Inflammatory markers drawn in your office in September were normal.

Impression: GCA in remission on prednisone 10 mg daily.
Plan: continue prednisone 10 mg daily. I will see him back in a year, sooner if symptoms recur.

Allergies: NKDA

Rheumatology

documents.title: Office Visit - Urinary Symptoms
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: getting up at night.

Over the fall he is up 3 or 4 times a night to void, more urgency during the day, and the stream is weaker than it used to be. Feels like he doesn't fully empty. No burning, no blood, no fevers, no back pain. Says it's like the BPH episode years ago, but worse. Cutting back fluids after dinner hasn't helped much.

Vitals charted, afebrile.
Abd soft, nontender, no suprapubic fullness. No CVA tenderness.
He prefers urology do the prostate exam since he'll be going anyway.

A/P: LUTS, likely recurrent BPH. Referral to urology. Avoid evening caffeine. Call if fever, retention or blood in urine.

OUTSIDE UROLOGY CONSULTATION
Visit date: 02/07/2023
Referring: primary care

Reason: lower urinary tract symptoms.

HPI: 70 y/o man with remote BPH, now several months of increasing urinary frequency and urgency, worst overnight with repeated waking to void. Stream is weak and he feels emptying is incomplete. Denies dysuria, gross hematuria, fever, or flank pain.

PMH: HTN, hyperlipidemia, CAD with stable angina, giant cell arteritis on prednisone, BPH. PSH: appendectomy, cholecystectomy.
Meds: aspirin 81, atorvastatin 40, amlodipine 5, prednisone 10.
Allergies: NKDA.
SH: never smoker, occasional alcohol.

Exam: vitals within normal limits. DRE: prostate symmetrically enlarged, smooth, no nodules, not tender.

Data: UA in clinic negative. Serum creatinine normal. Bladder scan post-void residual mildly elevated.

Impression: recurrent BPH with bothersome LUTS.
Plan: begin tamsulosin 0.4 mg at bedtime; reviewed dizziness on standing and to rise slowly. Return in 3 months to reassess symptoms and residual.

Urology

documents.title: Office Visit - Abdominal Pain
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: belly pain after eating.

Since around February he gets a crampy ache across the middle of his abdomen starting maybe half an hour after a meal and lasting a few hours. Worse after big meals. He has been eating less to avoid it, which he admits is why the weight is coming off. He didn't bring it up in May because he thought it was the new pills. Bowels regular, no blood, no black stools. No vomiting, no fever. Not related to the tamsulosin or lisinopril timing.

Weight 73 kg (80 last fall).
Abd: soft, mildly tender diffusely, no guarding, no mass, normal bowel sounds. No bruit appreciated.

A/P: postprandial abdominal pain with weight loss in a 71 y/o with CAD. Concern for a vascular cause among others. CBC, CMP, lipase today. GI referral, asked for a prompt appointment. Small, more frequent meals in the meantime. ER for severe or constant pain, blood in stool.

documents.title: Labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Blood count, liver tests, kidney function and lipase are all normal. That doesn't explain the pain, so GI is still the right next step. Your GI appointment is 8/1.

events.reason: Postprandial abdominal pain and weight loss

documents.title: Gastroenterology consultation
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
GASTROENTEROLOGY - NEW CONSULT
Date of service: 08/01/2023

Thank you for referring Mr. Graves, 71, with CAD and giant cell arteritis.

HPI: For about six months he has had diffuse cramping abdominal pain that comes on roughly 30 minutes after eating and lasts several hours. Not related to defecation. He has deliberately eaten less to avoid it and his weight is down 8 kg (80 to 72). No fever, vomiting or hematochezia.

PMH: HTN, hyperlipidemia, CAD/stable angina, GCA on prednisone, BPH. PSH: appendectomy, cholecystectomy.
Meds: aspirin 81, atorvastatin 40, lisinopril 20, amlodipine 5, prednisone 10, tamsulosin 0.4 qhs.
Allergies: NKDA. FH notable for paternal MI, maternal stroke, uncle with AAA. Never smoker.

Exam: thin older man, comfortable. Abdomen with mild diffuse tenderness, no guarding or rebound, no mass, bowel sounds present.

Labs: CBC and liver panel normal.

Assessment: the meal-related pain, food avoidance and weight loss in a man with diffuse atherosclerotic disease raise concern for intestinal ischemia from mesenteric arterial disease.

Plan:
1. CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis.
2. Colonoscopy with biopsies of any abnormal mucosa.
3. Small frequent low-fat meals.
Will update you with results.

Gastroenterology

reports.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
reports.text:
EXAM: CT angiography abdomen and pelvis.
INDICATION: postprandial abdominal pain, weight loss, suspected mesenteric ischemia.
TECHNIQUE: arterial and portal venous phase imaging after IV contrast, with multiplanar and 3D reformats.

FINDINGS:
Vascular: Calcified atherosclerotic plaque at the origins of the celiac axis and superior mesenteric artery without high-grade narrowing. Inferior mesenteric artery patent. Infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm measuring 4.4 cm in maximal outer-to-outer diameter, no periaortic stranding. Renal arteries patent. Iliac arteries of normal caliber with scattered calcification.
Bowel: no bowel wall thickening, pneumatosis or obstruction. Appendix not visualized, consistent with prior appendectomy.
Liver, spleen, pancreas, adrenals unremarkable. Cholecystectomy clips. Kidneys enhance symmetrically without hydronephrosis. Prostate enlarged. No adenopathy or free fluid.
reports.conclusion:
1. Mesenteric arterial origins with calcified plaque, no high-grade stenosis.
2. Infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm, 4.4 cm. Vascular surgery referral suggested.
3. No acute bowel abnormality.

documents.title: CTA report reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: CTA copy received from GI. Incidental 4.4 cm infrarenal AAA. No high-grade mesenteric stenosis. Called pt - he knew about the aneurysm from GI, colonoscopy is next week. Will set up vascular surgery after GI finishes. Added AAA to the problem list.

conditions.label: Ischemic colitis
conditions.note: Splenic flexure and proximal descending colon, biopsy-confirmed

reports.text:
SPECIMEN: colon, splenic flexure and proximal descending, biopsies (4 fragments).
MICROSCOPIC: colonic mucosa with withering crypts, lamina propria hyalinization and surface erosion with fibrinopurulent exudate. No granulomas, no dysplasia. No viral cytopathic effect.
reports.conclusion: Colonic mucosa with ischemic-type injury, consistent with ischemic colitis. Negative for dysplasia.

documents.title: Colonoscopy report
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
COLONOSCOPY
Date: 08/22/2023
Indication: postprandial abdominal pain, weight loss.
Sedation: monitored anesthesia care.
Prep: good.

Findings:
- Segmental mucosal edema and erythema with scattered shallow ulcerations from the splenic flexure into the proximal descending colon, with clear transitions to normal mucosa on either side. Biopsied.
- Remainder of the colon normal to the cecum. No polyps. Terminal ileum normal.

Pathology: ischemic-type mucosal injury, consistent with ischemic colitis.

Impression: ischemic colitis of the splenic flexure / proximal descending colon, in the setting of mesenteric atherosclerosis without high-grade stenosis on CTA.
Recommendations: small frequent low-fat meals; continue aspirin and statin; maintain blood pressure without overshooting low; vascular surgery referral for the AAA through primary care. No further screening colonoscopy needed at this time. GI follow-up as needed.

Gastroenterology

documents.title: Annual Wellness Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
AWV plus follow-up of the GI workup.

GI: colonoscopy 8/22 showed ischemic colitis at the splenic flexure, biopsy confirmed. CTA without a tight mesenteric stenosis, but a 4.4 cm infrarenal AAA. Eating 5 small meals a day now and the pain is much less, maybe a mild ache after a bigger dinner. Weight 73, holding.

Functional: independent. No falls. Still tutoring. Proxy on file.
PHQ-9 3 - a little down about the weight and all the appointments, sleeping fine, no thoughts of self-harm.

Exam: vitals charted. Thin. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender today. No pulsatile mass felt. Pedal pulses present.

A/P
1. Ischemic colitis - on problem list. Small meals, aspirin, statin. Avoid letting BP run low.
2. AAA 4.4 cm - vascular surgery referral. Uncle had one. He is a never smoker.
3. HTN controlled on lisinopril/amlodipine.
4. GCA on pred 10, rheum letter from January still not received; will re-request.
5. Colonoscopy this year doubles as his screening.
6. Flu and updated COVID in October.

Labs today. RTC 4 months.

documents.title: Vascular surgery consultation
documents.author: vascular surgery
documents.body:
VASCULAR SURGERY CONSULTATION - 11/07/2023

Reason: infrarenal AAA found on CTA in August done for abdominal pain.

Mr. Graves is a 71 y/o never smoker with HTN, hyperlipidemia, CAD, GCA on chronic prednisone and recently diagnosed ischemic colitis. Maternal uncle had an AAA. No back or abdominal pain beyond the meal-related discomfort, which is improving. No claudication.

Exam: BP and HR as recorded. Abdomen soft, aorta not clearly palpable. Femoral, popliteal and pedal pulses palpable bilaterally.

Imaging: I reviewed the CTA. Infrarenal aneurysm 4.4 cm with suitable neck anatomy. Mesenteric origins calcified without high-grade stenosis.

Assessment: asymptomatic 4.4 cm infrarenal AAA.
Plan: surveillance ultrasound in 12 months. Repair threshold 5.5 cm, or growth more than 1 cm per year, or symptoms. Continue aspirin and atorvastatin. Blood pressure control per PCP. Avoid fluoroquinolones. He knows to go to the ED for sudden severe abdominal or back pain.

Vascular Surgery

reports.text: Sinus rhythm, rate 68. Normal axis. PR, QRS and QT intervals normal. No ST elevation or depression. No pathologic Q waves. No change from the prior tracing in the cardiology records.
reports.conclusion: Normal sinus rhythm. No ischemic changes.

documents.title: Cardiology visit - groin
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
Outside cardiology - 02/16/2024

Seen for left groin discomfort and swelling for two weeks, starting a few days after his 2/2 diagnostic catheterization through the left femoral artery. That study showed moderate nonobstructive coronary disease with no lesion needing intervention; medical therapy continues.

He has CAD on chronic prednisone for GCA. Pain is mild. No leg swelling, numbness or coolness.

Vitals within normal limits.
Exam: small tender mass at the left groin access site with a palpable thrill and a continuous bruit. Distal pulses intact. Rest of exam unremarkable.

Labs: Hb 14.2, WBC 7.5, platelets 250, creatinine 1.0, BUN 18.

Arterial duplex of the left groin today: a small arteriovenous communication between the left common femoral artery and common femoral vein. No pseudoaneurysm. No hematoma of significance.

Impression: post-catheterization left femoral arteriovenous fistula, small.
Plan: observation, as many close on their own; repeat duplex with his vascular surgery surveillance. Return sooner for enlarging swelling, leg swelling or pain. Continue aspirin. Angina medical therapy unchanged.

Cardiology

REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER - EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
Arrival: 04/07/2024 13:20

CC: two weeks of feeling unwell, belly pain, painful purple legs, vision episodes.

HPI: 71 y/o man with GCA on prednisone, CAD, and a left groin AV fistula after a femoral cardiac catheterization 2/2. Over two weeks: progressive malaise, vague abdominal pain, a painful purplish discoloration of both legs, and several brief episodes of blurred or patchy vision in either eye lasting minutes. No headache, jaw claudication or scalp tenderness.

Meds: aspirin, atorvastatin, lisinopril, amlodipine 5, prednisone 10, tamsulosin 0.4. NKDA.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admit 02/05/2026  Discharge 02/17/2026
Services: critical care, cardiac surgery

Principal diagnosis: acute type A aortic dissection.

Presentation: 73 y/o man with CAD, GCA on chronic prednisone, AAA s/p EVAR (7/2025), prior mesenteric ischemia with ileal resection and cholesterol embolism. Two hours of sudden severe tearing chest pain through to the back with shortness of breath. BP 180/100 right arm, 160/90 left. Diastolic murmur best at the right second intercostal space. Labs: Hb 14, WBC 12.0, platelets 250, creatinine 1.2, troponin I <0.04 ng/mL. CXR widened mediastinum. ECG without ST changes or Q waves. CTA: dissection from just above the aortic valve through the arch into the descending thoracic aorta.

Procedure 02/05/2026: emergency replacement of the ascending aorta and hemiarch with aortic valve resuspension. Intraoperative TEE: moderate aortic regurgitation before repair, trivial after resuspension.

Course: ICU 4 days, extubated day 1. Stress-dose hydrocortisone then prednisone 10 mg resumed. Blood pressure and heart rate control with IV agents, then oral metoprolol succinate added. Femoral pulses palpable post-op. Creatinine stable. Ambulating independently at discharge.
